title: Full-size Bronco
eyebrow: FORD BRONCO · SECOND TO FIFTH GENERATION · 1978–1996
verdict: Ford took an F-Series four-by-four, cut a foot out of it and bolted on a roof you could lift off, and in doing so built the Bronco most people still picture. Simple pushrod engines, parts in every junkyard and a Twin Traction Beam front end that rewards anyone who owns an alignment gauge.

paragraphs: For 1978 Ford stopped pretending the Bronco was a small truck. The [[bronco/early-bronco|early Bronco]] had been a 92-inch-wheelbase box that fought the [[jeep/cj-5|CJ-5]] and the [[scout/scout-80-800|Scout]]; the new one was a shortened F-100 four-by-four aimed at the Chevrolet K5 Blazer, the Dodge Ramcharger and Jeep's two-door SJ Cherokee, cousin of the [[jeep/grand-wagoneer|Grand Wagoneer]]. Wikipedia's figures show what that meant: 12 inches more wheelbase, about 28 inches more length, 11 inches more width and between 1,100 and 1,600 pounds more weight, depending on the powertrain. In an era of downsizing, Ford went the other way on purpose, and it worked.

story.heading: 1978–79: PROJECT SHORTHORN
paragraphs: Development ran under the name Project Shorthorn and the truck was meant to launch for 1974. The 1973 fuel crisis pushed it back four years, so by the time the second-generation Bronco went on sale, its 1980 replacement was already nearly finished. Ford built it on the 1973–79 F-100 chassis with a 104-inch wheelbase, a coil-sprung Dana 44 front axle and a leaf-sprung Ford 9-inch rear. It was the last Bronco with a solid front axle until the nameplate went away. Part-time 4WD with a gear-driven New Process 205 was standard; a full-time, chain-driven NP203 was optional.

There was no six. The 351M V8 was standard and the 400 was optional, both two-barrel engines with about 156–158 hp; the 400 made 277 lb-ft against the 351M's 262. Doors, forward roof and dash came straight from the F-100, and Dick Nesbitt's lift-off fiberglass top covered only the area behind the B-pillars, with the seals designed to beat the leaks of the Blazer's top. The rear glass wound down into the tailgate. Demand was strong enough that buyers waited months, and Ford built 77,917 in 1978 and 104,038 in 1979, outselling the Blazer and the Ramcharger for the first time.

story.heading: 1980–86: TWIN TRACTION BEAM
paragraphs: The 1980 Bronco moved to the new seventh-generation F-150 but kept the 104-inch wheelbase. To chase fuel economy, Ford gave the 1980–81 trucks a lighter frame with holes stamped in it, saving 375 lb, then went back to a stronger frame for 1982. The big change was up front: a Dana 44 Twin Traction Beam, Ford's patented independent front drive axle. Each side pivots on its own beam, there is a U-joint in the middle, and the differential sits offset to the driver's side. Wikipedia sums up the reputation: unloved by some slow-speed crawlers, praised by high-speed desert racers.

Engines got smaller first. The 4.9-liter 300 inline-six became standard (manual only), the 302 V8 came back, the 400 was dropped and the 351M gave way to the 351 Windsor in 1982. A 210-hp high-output 351 arrived for 1984, and in 1985 the 302 gained multiport fuel injection and 190 hp. The blue oval replaced F-O-R-D lettering on the hood for 1982, and the Eddie Bauer package, with color-keyed two-tone paint, arrived for 1985. The rear axle went from the 9-inch to the 8.8 by the end of 1986.

story.heading: 1987–96: FUEL INJECTION, AIRBAGS AND A BOLTED-ON ROOF
paragraphs: The 1987 facelift brought the eighth-generation F-150 nose, composite headlights, a new dash and standard rear-wheel ABS. Fuel injection reached the 300 six for 1987 and the 351 for 1988, the year a Mazda-built M5OD five-speed manual and standard transfer-case skid plates also arrived. The C6 automatic gave way to the overdrive AOD and E4OD around 1990. For 1991, the Bronco's 25th year, the Silver Anniversary Edition brought exclusive Currant Red paint and the first leather seats in a Bronco.

The 1992 truck got a rounder ninth-generation nose. Four-wheel ABS followed for 1993, a driver's airbag for 1994, and the 300 six left the line-up, making every later Bronco a V8. Three-point rear belts and a center brake light now mounted in the hardtop, so Ford stopped describing top removal in the owner's manual and fastened the top with #40 security Torx bolts. The last Bronco left Wayne, Michigan, on June 12, 1996, and the four-door Expedition replaced it. Ford says the white 1993 Bronco on the 405 freeway in June 1994 had nothing to do with that decision, because sales were already falling.

story.heading: THE RESTOMOD ERA
paragraphs: Thirty years on, the full-size Bronco has become the affordable way into Bronco ownership and also a favorite donor for restomods. Bring a Trailer's 1978–79 page alone listed 263 auctions by October 2026. Prices run from a $14,000 1979 Ranger XLT to a Coyote-swapped 1979 Ranger XLT at $81,500. In August 2026 a 1979 Custom with a 7.3-liter Godzilla V8, a 10-speed automatic and Super Duty axles sold for $191,000. The 1987–96 trucks are the bargain: most ordinary XLTs and Eddie Bauers on BaT sell for between $7,500 and $32,500. They are simple and plentiful, and since 2021 they have shared the name with the [[bronco/sixth-gen|sixth-generation Bronco]], but they are still at their best covered in mud.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · THE FOUR-DOOR BRONCO
callout.title: Centurion's crew-cab Bronco
paragraphs: Ford built the 1978–96 Bronco only as a two-door, so Centurion Vehicles of White Pigeon, Michigan, made its own four-door. The Centurion Classic joined an F-Series crew cab (from the C-pillar forward) to the rear body of a Bronco (from the B-pillar back), including its quarter panels, hardtop and tailgate. It rode on a 140-inch wheelbase and seated up to nine.

The C-150 used an F-150 chassis with 5.0 or 5.8 V8s and optional 4WD. The C-350 used a one-ton F-350 with standard 4WD and either the 7.3 diesel or 7.5 gasoline V8, the only Broncos ever built with either engine. A 1994 C-350 Classic with the 7.5 was bid to $25,250 on Bring a Trailer in September 2026 without selling.

engineering_intro: Every full-size Bronco is a short-wheelbase F-Series. From the B-pillars forward it shares the pickup's cab, doors and dash, and behind them sits a three-door wagon body with a removable fiberglass top and a tailgate whose glass winds down into it. The chassis is a conventional ladder frame. The front axle changed from a solid Dana 44 to a Twin Traction Beam Dana 44 in 1980, and that change splits owners more than any other.

engineering.note: 1978–79 on the F-100, 1980 on the new F-150. The 1980–81 frame was lightened with stamped holes; 1982 went back to a stronger frame.

engineering.v: Dana 44 solid, coil springs (1978–79) · Dana 44 TTB (1980–96)
engineering.note: TTB is independent: two beams, a center U-joint, a slip yoke on the long side and the differential offset to the driver's side.
Wikipedia says Ford moved its half-ton trucks to the 8.8 by the end of 1986.

engineering.v: NP205 / NP203 (1978–79) · NP208 or BW1345 (from 1980) · BW1356 (later trucks)
engineering.note: Push-button electric shift was optional from 1987.
302 fuel-injected from 1985, 300 from 1987, 351 from 1988. The six was dropped after 1993.
From 1994 the top carries the rear seat-belt anchors and the third brake light, and is held on with #40 security Torx bolts.

generations_table.note: Solid coil-sprung Dana 44 front, 9-inch rear. T-18 or NP435 4-speed, or C6 automatic. NP205 part-time or NP203 full-time.
TTB Dana 44 front. 351W replaces 351M from 1982. Eddie Bauer package from 1985.
EFI on the 300 (1987) and 351 (1988). Rear ABS, M5OD 5-speed from 1988, E4OD from 1990. Silver Anniversary Edition for 1991.
4-wheel ABS 1993, driver airbag 1994, OBD-II 1996. The hardtop is bolted on with security Torx from 1994.

buying_checks.head: Rust in Ford's favorite places
buying_checks.body: Bronco Zone's long-time checklist names the inner rear fender lips, the bottoms of the B-pillars and the bottom of the tailgate, where spot-welded seams trap moisture. Also check the radiator core support where it bolts to the frame (mostly the passenger side), the floor around the rear seat-belt mounts, rain gutters, body mounts and the frame itself.

buying_checks.head: Run the tailgate glass both ways
buying_checks.body: Lower and raise the rear window from the key and from the dash switch, then open and close the tailgate. Check the tailgate drains and the outer glass seal. A window that works from only one control points to the circuit, not the motor. On many trucks the driver's window switch must be in the center position before the tailgate key switch will work.

buying_checks.head: Read the tires before the TTB
buying_checks.body: Uneven inner or outer tread wear means camber trouble. Look at the radius-arm bushings, which perish (one Bronco Zone owner replaced his at 80,000 miles), and check the ball joints and tie-rod ends. If the truck is lifted, ask whether adjustable camber bushings were fitted, because Bronco Graveyard says even 1–2-inch lift springs normally need them.

buying_checks.head: E4OD fluid and the O/D light
buying_checks.body: On 1990–96 automatics, the fluid should be red, not brown or burnt-smelling, and read full at operating temperature. A flashing overdrive light (TCIL) while driving means the transmission has stored a fault code. Owners recommend fluid and filter service every 30,000 miles, and sooner for towing.

buying_checks.head: Try 4-High and 4-Low
buying_checks.body: On push-button trucks, the shift motor and its connector are known trouble spots, often from a broken travel stop or a fouled connector. Ford recalled some 1993 trucks (93V-089) whose transfer cases had the wrong shift motor and could slip out of 4-High.

buying_checks.head: Compression, cooling and leaks
buying_checks.body: Owners call a bad compression or vacuum test a deal-breaker. The plastic side seams of the radiator leak, most visibly after the engine cools overnight. Check the rear main and timing-cover seals, look for a cracked exhaust manifold or Y-pipe, and check for water in the oil.

buying_checks.head: Decide whether you need a removable top
buying_checks.body: 1978–93 tops were designed to come off. From 1994 the top carries the rear three-point belts and the center brake light and is held with security Torx bolts. You can still remove it, but Wikipedia notes that driving without it can earn a ticket in some places.

buying_checks.head: Open recalls
buying_checks.body: Old trucks still show up with open campaigns. The 1994–96 speed-control deactivation switch (05V-388) and its 1993 equivalents (07V-336 and 08V-051) can overheat and burn, and 1988–91 trucks had an ignition-switch short-circuit recall (96V-071). Check the VIN on NHTSA's site.

repairs.title: Fix a tailgate window that won't move
repairs.cost: About $20 for a pair of regulator rollers (Wild Horses lists them at $9.99 each); a motor gear kit or a regulator costs more
repairs.symptoms: The rear glass won't go up or down, moves from the key but not the dash switch (or the other way round), or grinds and stalls part-way.
repairs.fix: First find out whether the motor or the circuit is at fault. Remove the tailgate access panel, find the motor connector near the bottom center of the opening, and power the motor directly from a battery with jumper leads; reversing the leads reverses it. If it runs, trace the circuit: the safety limit switch (in the latch handle on a 1980 truck), a corroded ground or broken wire, or the driver's window switch, which must be centered for the tailgate key switch to work. If the motor hums but the glass doesn't move, replace the nylon regulator gear with a gear kit. If the glass binds or cocks, replace both regulator-arm rollers that run in the lift channels under the glass, and lube the tracks with white lithium grease.
repairs.tools: Trim tools · screwdrivers · 12 V jumper leads · test light or meter · white lithium grease.

parts.name: Tailgate window regulator arm roller bushing, 1978–96 (SKU 796538, each)
1980–95 Bronco tailgate window motor gear repair kit
1980–96 Bronco inner and outer tailgate window seals

repairs.title: Correct TTB camber with adjustable bushings
repairs.symptoms: Tires wearing on the inner or outer edge, especially after new springs or a lift, and an alignment shop saying it's 'out of adjustment'.
repairs.fix: On a TTB Dana 44, camber is set by an offset bushing (sleeve) around the upper ball-joint stud. Bronco Graveyard describes the swap: remove the wheel, the cotter pin and the upper ball-joint nut, break the stud's taper free of the sleeve, pull the old sleeve with a sleeve puller and fit the new adjustable one. Adjustable sleeves cover 0.75 to 2.75 degrees, and any correction you don't need for camber can be turned into caster. Set both sides, torque the nuts, fit new cotter pins and have it aligned.
repairs.tools: Jack and stands · camber/caster sleeve puller · hammer or pickle fork · torque wrench · camber gauge (optional).

parts.name: 1980–96 Bronco and F-150 4WD adjustable alignment bushings (pair)

repairs.title: Replace radius-arm bushings
repairs.symptoms: A clunk over bumps or on braking, wandering steering and caster that won't hold. The rubber at the rear of each radius arm, where it passes through the frame bracket, is cracked or squashed out.
repairs.fix: Support the frame on stands with the axle on a jack so the arms are unloaded. Remove the nut at the rear end of each radius arm, slide off the washers and old bushings, and pry the arm down out of the bracket just far enough to fit the new bushings and washers. Bronco Graveyard's 1980–87 kit swaps the rubber for polyurethane and replaces the loose washers; adjustable bushings are available if you need to correct caster after a lift. Torque at ride height and get an alignment.
repairs.tools: Jack and stands · large sockets and breaker bar · pry bar · torque wrench.

parts.name: 1980–87 Bronco and F-Series radius-arm bushing repair kit (poly)
1980–97 Bronco and F-Series adjustable radius-arm bushing

repairs.title: Rebuild the TTB knuckle: spindle bearings, axle U-joints, ball joints
repairs.symptoms: Clunk or play at the front wheel, grease flung around the hub, a clicking U-joint when turning in 4WD, or a ball joint that moves when you lever the wheel top to bottom.
repairs.fix: With the hub and rotor off, unbolt the spindle and pull it to get at the outer axle shaft. Replace the spindle needle bearing and seals with a Spicer kit (1980–92 and 1994–96 kits differ), and replace the axle-shaft U-joints while the shafts are out; confirm the joint size for your shafts before ordering. If the ball joints are loose, press them out with a C-frame press and adapters, fit new Spicer joints, and reset the upper adjuster sleeve. Repack the wheel bearings, reassemble and set the bearing preload.
repairs.tools: Hub/spindle-nut socket · slide hammer or seal puller · ball-joint C-press and adapters · U-joint press or vise · torque wrench.

parts.name: 1980–92 Dana 44 TTB Spicer spindle bearing repair kit
1994–96 Ford Dana 44 TTB front-end rebuild kit
1980–96 TTB Dana 44 Spicer lower ball joint

repairs.title: Replace the TFI ignition module (1985–91 EFI)
repairs.symptoms: Hard hot starts, intermittent stalling that clears once the engine cools, misfires or erratic running on a fuel-injected V8.
repairs.fix: The Thick Film Ignition module bolts to the side of the distributor, close to the thermostat housing, where Bronco Graveyard says engine heat eventually kills it. Disconnect the battery, unplug the module, remove its two screws (a long T20 driver or Ford's module tool helps), and slide it off its terminals. Coat the mounting face of the new module with dielectric grease, which acts as a heat sink, and fit it. Bronco Graveyard recommends genuine Motorcraft modules and notes that many owners carry a spare on the trail.
repairs.tools: T20 Torx or Ford ignition-module tool · offset distributor clamp wrench (if the distributor has to come out) · dielectric grease.

parts.name: Ford Motorcraft V8 spark-plug wire set

repairs.title: Fix a push-button transfer case that won't shift
repairs.symptoms: The 4WD lights blink or the case won't go into (or out of) 4-High or 4-Low on an electric-shift truck.
repairs.fix: Bronco Zone owners point first at the shift motor and its connector: clean and reseat the connector and check for a broken travel stop. If the motor still doesn't respond, unbolt it from the BW1356, note the shift-shaft position and fit a new motor, replacing the shift seal while it's off. Match the new motor's position to the shift shaft before bolting it on. On a 1993 truck, check that recall 93V-089 (wrong shift motor) was done.
repairs.tools: Sockets · electrical contact cleaner · multimeter · new shift seal.

parts.name: Transfer-case actuating motor for BW1356 (Ford ref. E8TZ-7G360-B)
Motorcraft Mercon V automatic transmission fluid

repairs.title: Service the E4OD (1990–96)
repairs.symptoms: Late or harsh shifts, a flashing overdrive light, or dark, burnt-smelling fluid.
repairs.fix: Drop the pan, change the filter, clean the pan and magnet, and refill with Mercon V, which the factory manual quoted on Bronco Zone specifies for the E4OD. A pan drop only replaces about 8.5 of the roughly 16 quarts, so repeat the job, or add a drain plug or a deeper pan, to replace more of the old fluid. If you find particles or white (water-contaminated) fluid, get it diagnosed before you refill it. Read any stored codes if the O/D light flashes.
repairs.tools: Drain pan · sockets · gasket scraper · funnel · torque wrench.

parts.name: B&M Hi-Tek deep aluminum pan, E4OD/4R100
Motorcraft Mercon V automatic transmission fluid

repairs.title: Cut out and patch the rust
repairs.symptoms: Bubbling paint along the rear wheel-arch lips, holes at the bottom of the B-pillars or tailgate, a soft floor near the rear seat-belt anchors, a rotted radiator core support.
repairs.fix: Bronco Zone owners blame Ford's spot-welded seams, which trap water, so the rust usually runs further than it looks. Strip back to clean steel, cut the panel out beyond the rot, and butt-weld in a patch or a full panel. Seam-seal, prime and paint, and treat the inside with cavity wax. On the tailgate, clear the drains and fit new internal hardware while it's apart.
repairs.tools: Cut-off wheel · MIG welder · flap discs · panel clamps · seam sealer · cavity wax.

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: A 33-inch tire. On Bronco Zone, one moderator ran 33x12.50R15s on 15x10 wheels on a stock-height 1986 with no rubbing; another owner said 33s fit without a lift but snugly, sometimes needing the bumper ends trimmed or shimmed, with slight radius-arm rub depending on the wheel. For 35s, a 3-inch body lift is the bare minimum, a 4-inch suspension lift is better and 6 inches is ideal. 38s need about 6 inches plus serious fender trimming. Check your axle ratio before going bigger.

faq.q: Which years should I look at?
faq.a: It depends what you want, because there's no consensus best year: Bronco Zone owners argue engines (the 351 'feels like a truck motor', the 302 is smoother) and OBD-I versus OBD-II rather than model years. The 1978–79 trucks are the only ones with a solid front axle and 400 V8s, and they bring the most money. The 302 got fuel injection in 1985, the 351 and the five-speed manual came in 1988, and four-wheel ABS and a driver's airbag followed in 1993 and 1994. From 1994 the top is effectively fixed, and the 1996 trucks have OBD-II diagnostics.

faq.q: Can I take the hardtop off?
faq.a: Yes on 1978–93 trucks, which were built for it. From 1994 the top carries the rear three-point belts and the third brake light, so Ford removed the instructions from the owner's manual and fastened the top with #40 security Torx bolts. It still comes off, but driving without it can mean inoperable rear belts and a missing brake light, and in some states a ticket.

faq.q: Is Twin Traction Beam bad off-road?
faq.a: It's divisive. TTB was Ford's attempt to combine solid-axle simplicity with independent-suspension ride, and Wikipedia notes that slow-speed crawlers tend to dislike it while high-speed racers praise it. The practical issue is that camber changes with ride height, so lifted trucks need adjustable camber bushings: Bronco Graveyard says they're normally needed even with 1–2-inch lift springs.

faq.q: What oil and fluids does it take?
faq.a: The 1996 shop manual, quoted on Bronco Zone, prefers 5W-30 in all climates. AMSOIL's capacity lookup for a 1992 5.8 lists 6 quarts with the filter. The E4OD and BW1356 transfer case take Mercon V; AMSOIL lists 16.2 quarts total (about 8.5 on a pan drop) for a 4WD E4OD, and 4 pints for the 1356. The 8.8 rear takes 80W-90 (Ford XY-80W90-QL), about 5.5 pints, plus 4 oz of Ford friction modifier in a Traction-Lok. Coolant is a 50/50 ethylene-glycol mix. The 1996 workshop manual adds Mercon ATF for the Mazda five-speed (3.8 quarts), Ford 4x4 gear oil for the Dana 44 front (3.6 pints) and Ford Premium Power Steering Fluid for the pump.
faq.src: 1996 FORD WORKSHOP MANUAL · BRONCO ZONE · AMSOIL

faq.a: The 1978–79 Bronco and early third-generation trucks have the leaf-sprung Ford 9-inch. Ford moved its half-ton trucks to the 8.8 by the end of 1986, so most later Broncos have the 8.8. If it matters to you, confirm which axle a given truck has from its axle tag or with the seller.

faq.q: Can I get one with a manual gearbox?
faq.a: Yes, through 1996. The 1978–79 trucks offered Borg-Warner T-18 or New Process 435 four-speeds, and the 300 six was manual-only in the early 1980s. A Mazda-built M5OD five-speed arrived for 1988. The 1991 Silver Anniversary and Nite editions, and the Eddie Bauer, came only with a V8 and an automatic.

Wikipedia's year-by-year figures add up to about 902,500: 181,955 in 1978–79, 322,429 in 1980–86, 235,451 in 1987–91 and 162,703 in 1992–96. Treat the total as approximate, because the table repeats identical figures for 1983–84 and for 1987–88.

faq.q: Did the O.J. Simpson chase kill the Bronco?
faq.a: No, according to Ford. Al Cowlings's white 1993 Bronco XLT made the June 17, 1994 chase famous, but Ford said sales were already declining. The Expedition replaced the Bronco for 1997, and the last one was built on June 12, 1996.

On Bring a Trailer in 2025–26, ordinary 1987–96 trucks mostly sold for $7,500 to $32,500, and the best Eddie Bauers and celebrity-owned trucks went higher (a 1995 Eddie Bauer sold for $67,500). 1980–86 trucks ran from a $7,750 project to $50,000. The 1978–79 trucks are the most expensive: stock examples sold for about $14,000 to $49,000, and big-engine restomods sold for $80,000 to $191,000.

mods.why: Taller coils up front and longer shackles or springs at the rear make room for 35s. On a TTB truck, plan for camber bushings and radius-arm work at the same time.
Adjustable camber/caster sleeves and poly radius-arm bushings are the cheapest way to make a lifted TTB truck drive straight and stop eating tires.

who.name: Bronco Graveyard — bushings, rubber and polyurethane

mods.why: Bigger tires find the weak spots in TTB shafts and U-joints, and the aftermarket sells chromoly and CV axle sets for the half-ton Dana 44.
Open front differentials and tall highway gears were the norm, so a locker and lower gears go together with bigger tires.
This is the restomod route: Coyote and Godzilla swaps at the top of the market, and the older big-block 460 swap for a simpler build.
A two-ton-plus short-wheelbase truck on 33s or 35s needs a winch and real recovery points before it needs light bars.

who.name: Bronco Graveyard — recovery straps and winches

baseline_service.intro: These are thirty-year-old trucks with simple pushrod engines, so assume nothing has been done and baseline every fluid. Treat the front axle as a service item too. The TTB's spindle bearings, U-joints, ball joints and radius-arm bushings decide how the truck drives, and on most Broncos for sale they're original.

items.spec: SAE 5W-30 preferred in all climates (Ford ESE-M2C153-E); 10W-30 acceptable in hot weather · 6 qt with filter (1992 5.8)
items.interval: Then every 5,000 mi, or every 3,000 mi on Ford's severe-duty schedule (1996 workshop manual)
items.note: Drain-plug torque 15–25 ft-lb (AMSOIL lookup). Owners of tired, high-mileage engines often move to thicker oils.

items.interval: Check every oil change; Ford's 1996 schedule replaces it every 30,000 mi or 30 months, sooner in dust
items.note: Check the airbox seal and the intake tube after any trail trip.

items.item: Ignition: plugs, cap, rotor, wires, TFI
items.spec: 1996 workshop manual: 5.8 Motorcraft ASF-32C, gap 0.042–0.046 in · 5.0 ASF-42P, gap 0.052–0.056 in · 4.9 BSF-44C, gap 0.042–0.046 in. Check the VECI decal on earlier trucks
items.interval: Baseline once; Ford's 1996 schedule replaces plugs at 60,000 mi
items.note: On 1985–91 EFI trucks, inspect the distributor-mounted TFI module and fit any replacement with dielectric grease as a heat sink.

parts.name: Spark plugs, cap and rotor, 1992 Bronco

items.spec: Ethylene glycol, 50/50 premix · 14.8–15.9 qt (1992 5.8, by transmission and A/C)
items.interval: Flush at purchase, then every 30,000 mi or 36 months (Ford 1996 schedule; first change from new at 50,000 mi/48 months)
items.note: Check the plastic side seams of the radiator, which tend to leak after the engine cools overnight.

parts.name: Bronco Graveyard — heating and cooling systems

items.spec: Mercon V · 16.2 qt total, ≈ 8.5 qt on a pan drop (4WD E4OD)
items.interval: Fluid and filter every 30,000 mi (owners' recommendation); sooner if towing
items.note: A single pan drop replaces only about half the fluid. C6 (13.5 qt total) and AOD (12.3 qt) trucks: use the fluid stamped on the dipstick.

items.spec: Motorcraft MERCON ATF · 3.8 qt (7.6 pints) for the Mazda R2 five-speed (1996 workshop manual); AMSOIL lists 6.8–7.6 pints
items.interval: Drain and refill at purchase; Ford changes it every 60,000 mi
items.note: Owners recommend resealing the rubber plugs in the M5OD shift cover, which shrink and leak. Check the slave cylinder for leaks.

items.spec: BW1356: Mercon V (factory manual), ≈ 4 pints · BW1345: ≈ 6.3 pints
items.note: AMSOIL notes Ford has since updated the spec to Mercon LV. On push-button cases, clean the shift-motor connector while you're under there.

items.spec: Ford 4x4 Gear Oil F1TZ-19580-A (WSL-M2C191-A) · 3.6 pints for the Dana 44 IFS (1996 workshop manual, F-150/Bronco). The manual's table doesn't state a viscosity, so match the Ford spec
items.interval: Change at purchase and after deep water
items.note: Check the axle vent tube, and look for gear oil weeping from the slip-yoke seal on the long side of a TTB.

items.spec: SAE 80W-90 (Ford XY-80W90-QL, WSP-M2C197-A) · ≈ 5.5 pints (8.8 Traction-Lok) plus 4 oz Ford friction modifier (F3TZ-19B546-MA)
items.note: Fill to 1/4–9/16 inch below the filler hole (factory manual via Bronco Zone). Seal the 8.8 cover with silicone (D6AZ-19562-AA or equivalent).

items.item: Front wheel bearings, spindle bearings & hubs
items.spec: Ford High Temperature 4x4 Front Axle and Wheel Bearing Grease E8TZ-19590-A (ESA-M1C198-A), which the 1996 manual also specifies for the spindle needle bearings and axle U-joints
items.note: On a TTB truck, do the spindle needle bearings and seals and the axle U-joints while the hub is apart.

items.spec: Radius-arm bushings · ball joints · tie-rod ends
items.note: Have a helper rock the steering wheel while you watch each joint. Perished radius-arm bushings are common.
